syntax: The nominative naṭa and its nominal descriptor nāṭyadhara share the actor in the comparee clause. The analogy licenses that case on its actor sense.
contact: The nominal-ending s becomes ru; after short a before n it receives u under 6.1.114. Then 6.1.87 gives o.
observations: Unnumbered anyebhyo ’pi dṛśyante appears after the potter/hireling gloss inside IV.107 on p. 54. Numbered IV.108 begins the next kuṣ rule.
A separately numbered 4.105 starts on the same printed page after the 4.104 roster. The next kuṣ rule is 4.106.
The explicitly segmented roster prints sya, ṭha, ḍaṭa and aṭac in sequence, with other explicit virāmas before those final members. Separating the suffix words preserves the short ninth label.
The printed ḍit–ṭi-lopa explanation precedes naṭa in both witnesses. Ujjvaladatta additionally gives the stage performer gloss.
Two independently recorded lexical analyses give the performer, with nam+ḍaṭa and naṭ+aC kept distinct.
The 1.8.19 simile has the nominative actor under the nāṭyadhara descriptor and shows the expected joined o.
decisions: Accept both historical locations of the extension. Compare a rule by its wording and adjacency as well as ordinal. The printed difference does not attest an untracked direct import lineage.
In the 1859 expansion accept short aṭac and ḍaṭa with its ending vowel. The distinct ṭha and primary ḍha keep separate labels. No inherited 4.105 slot is replaced on this evidence.
Derive selected naṭa with the affix’s sounded ṭ. Preserve the separately named naṭ+aC and its exact lexical-scope obligations.
Neither printed boundary nor the earlier short-a assignments establish the four literal words for the primary extension. Leave them Open at 99/103.
morphology: ṭi of nam lost with ḍit, sounded aṭa retains ṭ
